3.         The Committee desired that final replies in respect of the recommendations, which have been categorized as

4.         On scrutiny of the said Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each item of the action
 taken/proposed to be taken by the Ministry.  The recommendations of the Committee contained in the Fifty-eighth
 Report, action taken thereon by the Government and recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of
 action taken have been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
 
AIR INDIA
(Recommendation at Para 15)
 
5.         The Committee, in its 42
nd Report on Demands for Grants 2000-2001 of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, had
 expressed hope that the rationalization of fleet with less types of aircraft will help reduce the demand for investment
 and spares, maintenance facilities and simulators and will also result in better utilization of aircraft infrastructural
 facilities and technical manpower of pilots and maintenance engineers.  The Committee, however, notes that while an
 expert committee has been set up to assess Air India's long term fleet requirements but no time-frame has been given to
 the Committee within which it should submit its recommendations.  The aircraft are required to be acquired during the
 Tenth five Year Plan Period, that is, 2002-2007.  In fact, a decision on this should have been completed by now so that
 by the time the Tenth Plan commenced, the Air India had started acquisition of the type of aircraft it proposed to
 acquire during this period. The Committee, therefore, reiterates the Recommendation made in its earlier report that the
 Air India decide in time bound manner and keep the Committee fully apprised as to what kind of fleet it should go in
 for so that necessary steps may be taken immediately to rationalise their fleet.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
6.         The Expert Committee constituted to develop Air India’s fleet plans for the next five years has submitted an
 interim report to the Managing Director, Air India for his consideration.  The interim report has given the details and
 rationale of the proposed pattern of operations to be achieved by the year 2007-08.  However, the report has indicated
 that a preliminary viability study would have to be undertaken to ascertain profitability of the system and based on the
 study, the pattern of operations would have to be reviewed.  The Expert Committee is in the process of taking up
 further studies to determine the economic viability.  The Committee is also in the process of deciding the ground rules
 and service standards to be offered in the new aircraft and has opened a dialogue with the aircraft manufactures to get
 the required data for this purpose.  The Committee would then obtain proposals from the manufactures and evaluate the
 candidate aircraft types.  They have estimated that this work will be completed by 30
th October 2002. 
 
7.         However, in the interim, Air India has inducted aircraft capacity on dry lease for growth and fleet
 rationalization.  Air India has progressively reduced the utilization of the older B747-200 aircraft.  This aircraft type
 will be phased out after Air India is able to certify a VVIP configuration on the B747-400 aircraft.
 
8.         Air India also proposes to phase out its three A300-B4 aircraft shortly.  Air India has already inducted five
 A310-300 aircraft on dry lease and will shortly induct another three A310-300 on dry lease to replace the A300-B4
 capacity.
 
9.         There have been certain developments in the Civil Aviation environment which call for caution in the medium
 term.  These developments are:-
 
(i)
                              Economic recession in the international markets from 2001;
(ii)                            The September 11, 2001 incident and its impact on Civil Aviation
(iii)                           The closure of Pakistani air space which has put Air India in disadvantage vis-à-vis its competitors on
 the West of India Routes.

 bail out package for their airlines.  Air India has registered a net profit in 2001-02.  This could be attributed to lower

40        The Committee observes that both Air India and Indian Airlines have a very low equity base.  Indian Airlines

 curtailing their borrowing ability.  It is of immediate necessity to enhance the equity base of both the airlines to enable
 them to achieve a healthy debt-equity ratio, and also enable them to go in for further borrowings.  The Committee has
 been informed that a commitment has already been made by the Ministry of Finance to contribute to the equity of
 Indian Airlines linking it to the acquisition of aircraft.  The Committee recommends that similar dispensation would be
 necessary for Air India as well.  The Committee appreciates the decision of the Government to strengthen the airlines
 instead of going in for disinvestment as stated by the Secretary in his deposition before the Committee.  For this
 purpose, the Committee feels that the Ministry should also come up with the proposal of financial restructuring, if
 necessary, for both the airlines.
 
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
 
41.       Ministry of Civil Aviation had earlier constituted a Committee under the Chairmanship of Dr. Vijay Kelkar, the
 then Secretary, Ministry of Petroleum in 1995, to look into the reasons for losses in Indian Airlines and to develop
 strategies to turn around Indian Airlines in the context of competitive market environment.  The Committee submitted
 its report in 1996.  The Committee had, inter-alia, recommended for financial support of Rs.922 crores out of which
 Rs.509 crores were to be from the Government and Rs.413 crores to be contributed by Indian Airlines and its
 employees.  The break-up of Rs.509 crores to be contributed by Government of India was as follows:-
 
(a)
                Rs.150 crores in the form of subordinated debt.
(b)               Rs.125 crores as equity infusion.
(c)                Rs.200 crores as compensation for grounding of A-320 aircraft &
(d)               Rs.34 crores as saving as a result of rationalization of ATF prices.
 
42.       These recommendations had been examined in detail and it was decided by the Government to release a sum of
 Rs.325 crores to Indian Airlines as equity in the form of margin money for acquisition of aircraft.
 
43.       In the meantime, the phased investment of Indian Airlines, bringing down Government’s holding to 49% over a
 period of three years, was announced in the Budget speech of 1998-99.  The funds approved for Indian Airlines could
 not be released because Ministry of Finance was of the opinion that it would not be prudent for Government to go on
 for disinvestments of 51% of the existing equity and at the same time infuse additional equity to the Company and
 advised that Indian Airlines would explore other options like leasing etc., for meeting its operational needs and restrict
 the proposal for acquisition to a bare minimum.
           
44.       It was however, agreed in principle to release a sum of Rs.325 crores as equity infusion in the form of margin
